domain.name: Finance & Business Analytics
domain.description: Practical bookkeeping, financial statements, budgeting, cash forecasting, profitability, working capital, controls, and scenario analysis for operating a business responsibly.

competencies.name: Bookkeeping Fundamentals
competencies.description: Record business activity consistently so financial reports reflect what actually happened.
competencies.purpose: Create trustworthy operating data before attempting higher-level analysis.

units.title: Transactions need classification and evidence
units.content: A useful bookkeeping record identifies date, amount, account/category, counterparty, business purpose, and supporting evidence. The same transaction should not be classified differently month to month just to make reports look better.

units.title: Monthly bookkeeping close
units.content: Collect bank and payment-platform activity; categorize revenue and expenses consistently; reconcile accounts to statements; identify transfers and owner transactions separately; attach supporting documents where available; review uncategorized items; then lock or mark the period complete before analysis.

units.title: Bookkeeping failures
units.content: Avoid mixing personal and business spending without clear classification, counting transfers as revenue, ignoring processor fees, duplicating imported transactions, leaving cash expenses undocumented, and changing categories to force a desired profit number.

drills.title: Close a small-business month
drills.prompt: Given bank deposits, card spending, a transfer between accounts, processor fees, an owner draw, and one cash purchase, explain how each should be classified and what evidence is needed before closing the month.

competencies.name: Financial Statements
competencies.description: Read income statements, balance sheets, and cash-flow statements as connected views of the business.
competencies.purpose: Understand performance, financial position, and cash movement without confusing one with another.

units.title: Three statements answer different questions
units.content: The income statement shows revenue and expenses over a period; the balance sheet shows assets, liabilities, and equity at a point in time; the cash-flow statement explains how cash changed. Profit, net worth, and cash are related but not interchangeable.

units.title: Financial statement review order
units.content: Review revenue and gross margin trends; inspect operating expenses and net income; then examine receivables, payables, debt, cash, and equity; reconcile why cash changed differently from profit; finally investigate unusual movements rather than reading only the bottom line.

units.title: Statement interpretation failures
units.content: Avoid treating revenue as profit, treating profit as cash, ignoring receivables that may never collect, ignoring debt-funded cash increases, comparing periods with different scopes, and drawing conclusions from one ratio without operating context.

drills.title: Explain the financial story
drills.prompt: A company shows rising revenue and positive net income but falling cash and rising receivables. Explain the likely operating story and what additional questions you would ask.

competencies.name: Budgeting
competencies.description: Turn priorities into explicit spending and revenue assumptions that can be compared with actual results.
competencies.purpose: Allocate limited resources intentionally instead of reacting after money is already spent.

units.title: A budget is a decision model
units.content: A useful budget links expected activity to money. It should show assumptions, fixed costs, variable costs, discretionary spending, contingency, and target outcomes. A budget is not a promise that every estimate will be correct.

units.title: Build an operating budget
units.content: Start with committed obligations; estimate revenue by source and timing; separate fixed and variable costs; include taxes/reserves as appropriate to the business context; allocate discretionary spending to priorities; add contingency; then compare actual versus budget monthly and explain material variance.

units.title: Budget scarce cash before optional ambition
units.content: Fund obligations, delivery capacity, and risk reserves before expansion spending. A high-return idea that threatens payroll, rent, taxes, or delivery reliability can still be a bad timing decision.

drills.title: Build a lean monthly budget
drills.prompt: A small service business expects uneven monthly revenue. Build a budget framework that protects fixed obligations, delivery costs, taxes/reserves, marketing, owner pay, and contingency without assuming every month is average.

competencies.name: Cash Forecasting
competencies.description: Forecast when money is expected to enter and leave, not only how much revenue or profit is expected.
competencies.purpose: See cash shortfalls early enough to change timing, collections, spending, or commitments.

units.title: Timing drives liquidity
units.content: A profitable job can still create a cash problem when expenses are paid before the client pays. Forecasting should model actual payment dates, deposits, collections probability, recurring bills, payroll, taxes, debt service, and one-time costs.

units.title: 13-week cash forecast
units.content: Start with current available cash; list expected inflows by week and confidence; list mandatory outflows by week; add planned discretionary outflows separately; calculate weekly ending cash; flag minimum-cash breaches; update actuals and revised timing at least weekly.

units.title: Cash forecast failures
units.content: Avoid placing invoice date where payment date belongs, assuming every receivable collects on time, ignoring annual or quarterly obligations, counting unused credit as cash without noting debt consequences, and updating the forecast only after a problem occurs.

drills.title: Diagnose a coming cash gap
drills.prompt: A business has cash today, two large invoices due to be collected next month, and payroll plus vendor bills due this month. Explain how to forecast the gap and identify non-destructive options before borrowing.
rubric: Debt is not automatic first answer

competencies.name: Break-Even Analysis
competencies.description: Calculate the activity level required to cover fixed costs given contribution margin.
competencies.purpose: Understand whether pricing and volume assumptions can support the cost structure.

units.title: Contribution margin funds fixed costs
units.content: Contribution margin equals revenue minus costs that vary with delivering that revenue. Break-even volume depends on fixed cost divided by contribution per unit or job. The calculation is only as useful as the cost behavior assumptions behind it.

units.title: Break-even workflow
units.content: Define the unit of sale; identify price; estimate variable cost per unit; calculate contribution; identify period fixed costs; compute break-even units or revenue; then test sensitivity to lower price, higher variable cost, and lower capacity.

units.title: Break-even failures
units.content: Avoid treating semi-variable labor as fixed without thought, ignoring capacity limits, using average margin when product mix varies heavily, excluding owner labor entirely, and using break-even as a profit target instead of the minimum point before profit.

drills.title: Calculate service break-even
drills.prompt: A service sells for $500, has $180 of variable delivery cost, and the business has $3,200 of monthly fixed cost. Calculate simple break-even jobs and explain which assumptions should be stress-tested.
rubric: Break-even not confused with target profit

competencies.name: Working Capital
competencies.description: Manage receivables, payables, inventory, deposits, and short-term obligations so operations have enough cash to function.
competencies.purpose: Prevent growth from consuming more cash than the business can support.

units.title: Growth can consume cash
units.content: When sales grow faster than collections, inventory turns, or supplier terms, more cash can become trapped in receivables or inventory. Working-capital management focuses on the timing gap between paying for delivery and collecting from customers.

units.title: Working-capital review
units.content: Measure days to collect receivables; identify overdue accounts; review deposit policy; review supplier payment terms; identify slow-moving inventory if relevant; compare customer payment timing with vendor/payment timing; then target the largest timing mismatch.

units.title: Fix the cash cycle before financing it
units.content: Before adding debt to solve recurring cash shortages, determine whether deposits, collections discipline, pricing, inventory, or payment terms can shorten the operating cash cycle.

drills.title: Improve a growth cash cycle
drills.prompt: A service business is booking more work but paying subcontractors weeks before clients pay final invoices. Propose changes to deposits, milestones, collections, and supplier terms before considering external financing.
rubric: Financing is not first-line by default

competencies.name: Accounts Receivable & Payable
competencies.description: Manage money owed by customers and money owed to vendors with clear aging, follow-up, and priority rules.
competencies.purpose: Protect cash, relationships, and record accuracy while reducing surprises.

units.title: Receivables discipline
units.content: Invoice promptly; state due date and payment instructions clearly; reconcile payments; review aging at least weekly; contact overdue customers consistently; document disputes; separate collection status from emotional assumptions; and escalate according to agreed policy or contract.

units.title: Payables discipline
units.content: Record bills when incurred; verify amount and vendor; track due dates; separate disputed charges; prioritize according to legal/contractual obligation, continuity of critical supply, penalties, and cash availability; avoid paying early automatically when cash is constrained unless there is a justified benefit.

units.title: AR/AP failures
units.content: Avoid invoicing late, leaving due dates ambiguous, applying payments to the wrong invoice, paying duplicate vendor bills, using collections as a memory-based process, ignoring small overdue balances until they accumulate, and stretching critical vendors without communication.

drills.title: Run an aging review
drills.prompt: Given invoices current, 15 days late, 45 days late, disputed, and partially paid, prioritize follow-up and define the next action for each status.

competencies.name: Margin & Profitability Analysis
competencies.description: Measure whether customers, services, jobs, and channels create enough contribution after real delivery cost.
competencies.purpose: Find where revenue creates value and where busy work hides weak economics.

units.title: Revenue quality matters
units.content: Two jobs with the same price can produce different profit because labor, subcontractors, revisions, travel, payment fees, usage, returns, and support differ. Profitability analysis should use the cost drivers that actually change by job or customer.

units.title: Job profitability review
units.content: Capture quoted price and collected revenue; record direct labor time, subcontractors, materials, travel, platform/processing fees, and other variable delivery cost; calculate contribution and effective hourly return; compare estimated versus actual; then identify scope, pricing, or process causes of variance.

units.title: Profitability failures
units.content: Avoid calling a job profitable because cash came in, ignoring unpaid revision time, using revenue per hour without direct costs, spreading all overhead equally when it obscures decision-useful differences, and keeping low-margin work only because it is familiar.

drills.title: Analyze an underperforming job
drills.prompt: A $900 job took 12 hours instead of 7 and included $140 of direct costs plus $35 in payment fees. Analyze the job and identify whether the fix belongs in price, scope, estimation, or process.

competencies.name: Scenario Analysis
competencies.description: Compare plausible outcomes under changing price, demand, cost, timing, and capacity assumptions.
competencies.purpose: Make decisions that remain useful when the future does not match the base forecast.

units.title: Forecast ranges beat false precision
units.content: Scenario analysis should separate assumptions from outputs. A base case, downside case, and upside case are useful when they reflect plausible changes in demand, price, cost, timing, and capacity rather than arbitrary percentage changes.

units.title: Build a decision scenario
units.content: Define the decision; identify the few assumptions that drive the result; create plausible downside/base/upside values; calculate cash, margin, and capacity implications; identify trigger points that would change the decision; then choose an action that is robust across more than one scenario when possible.

units.title: Stress the assumption that can kill the plan
units.content: Do not spend equal time varying every input. Find the assumption whose failure would make the plan unacceptable and stress-test that first.

drills.title: Scenario-test an equipment purchase
drills.prompt: A business is considering equipment based on expected monthly jobs. Build downside, base, and upside cases using job volume, contribution per job, financing/payment cost, and resale/exit considerations.
rubric: No single-point forecast treated as certainty

competencies.name: Financial Controls & Review
competencies.description: Use approvals, reconciliations, separation of duties, documentation, and exception review to reduce preventable loss and reporting errors.
competencies.purpose: Protect the business without creating unnecessary bureaucracy.

units.title: Controls should target meaningful failure modes
units.content: Useful controls reduce the chance or impact of error, fraud, duplicate payment, unauthorized spending, missing revenue, or inaccurate reporting. Controls should be proportional to the risk and volume involved.

units.title: Basic small-business control set
units.content: Separate request, approval, payment, and reconciliation when practical; require evidence for expenses; use spending limits; reconcile bank and processor accounts; review unusual vendors or amount changes; protect account access; document refunds and credits; and review exceptions rather than every low-risk transaction manually.

units.title: Control failures
units.content: Avoid one person creating vendors and approving their own payments without review, shared credentials, unreconciled accounts, undocumented cash handling, approval after payment, blanket vendor trust without amount verification, and controls so burdensome that people bypass them.

drills.title: Design a payment control flow
drills.prompt: Design a lightweight control process for vendor bills in a small business. Include invoice receipt, verification, approval threshold, payment, reconciliation, and handling of urgent exceptions.
